source: Momentum through the collision, energy after it: the carts stick, lose kinetic energy, then climb a ramp.
Students use energy conservation across a sticking collision, where kinetic energy is lost.

Two stages, two laws. During a quick collision the outside forces are small, so momentum is conserved. After it, on a smooth ramp, energy is conserved. The trap is to use energy across the collision itself. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.

Sticking collision: $$\role{mass}{m_1}\role[speed before]{velocity}{v} = (\role{mass}{m_1} + \role{mass}{m_2})\role[speed after]{velocity}{V}.$$ Kinetic energy is lost: the fraction lost is $\dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ when $m_2$ starts at rest. After the collision: $\tfrac{1}{2}V^2 = gh$, so $h = \dfrac{V^2}{2g}$.
Momentum carries the pair through the collision; energy carries it up the ramp.
Cart A ($0.6\ \text{kg}$, $3.0\ \text{m/s}$) locks onto cart B ($0.4\ \text{kg}$, at rest). Find (1) their speed, (2) the kinetic energy lost and (3) how high they roll up a smooth ramp.

Using $\tfrac{1}{2}m_1v^2 = (m_1 + m_2)gh$ straight from the start. That ignores the energy lost when the carts stick, so the height comes out too large. Check: an answer above $v^2/2g$ is impossible.
